en: The national flower, Sampaguita, blooms year-round and releases its sweet fragrance most strongly at night to attract pollinating moths.
The Philippine Eagle, our national bird, uses its dark facial crest to shield its eyes from the sun while hunting in the canopy.
The Ifugao people carved the Banaue Rice Terraces into the mountains, using a gravity-fed irrigation system called muyong to channel forest water downhill.
During Lucban's Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate their homes with kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from pounded green rice and natural food coloring.
Filipino scientist Angel Alcala pioneered coral reef restoration by sinking concrete blocks in Apo Island to provide hard surfaces for new coral polyps to grow.
The Narra, our national tree, drops its small, winged seed pods in the dry season so the wind can carry them to new growing locations.
While exiled in Dapitan, Jose Rizal built a water system by tapping a natural mountain spring and using local bamboo pipes to deliver clean water.
The T'boli people weave their sacred T'nalak cloth from abaca fibers, which they extract from the stalks of the native Musa textilis banana plant.
The carabao, our national animal, cools itself by wallowing in muddy water because it lacks sufficient sweat glands to regulate its body temperature.
In Morong, Bataan, locals protect the Pawikan marine turtles by monitoring the beaches where the endangered reptiles return annually to lay their eggs.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources enforces the National Greening Program, which requires planting native tree species to restore deforested mountain watersheds.
Andres Bonifacio and the Katipuneros initiated their secret society rites inside the Pamitinan Cave, using the natural stalactites and dripping spring water for their rituals.
